newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Cambodia's young bureaucrats brush up for ASEAN.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cambodia's young bureaucrats brush up for ASEAN.

text.p: The courses sound like an odd mix of academe and charm school -- international relations, personal grooming, advanced English and dining with diplomats.
But for Cambodia's budding young bureaucrats, this eclectic education makes perfect sense.
They want to be prepared for their country's imminent entry into the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), and they realise they still have a wide range of lessons to learn.

"The training is very good, very difficult," says Bun Neary, 23, a young woman who recently returned to work at the Ministry of Finance's ASEAN unit after two and a half months of intensive study in Malaysia.

"It was hard to learn to eat food (properly) and also to have conversations with diplomats. We were afraid we were lower than them," she says, describing nightly drills where she conversed with ASEAN diplomats over complicated table settings.
By day, Bun Neary says she learned English, ASEAN affairs, negotiating skills, the framework of international trade agreements and the structure of world lending agencies.
It's a broad and ambitious course of study, but in Cambodia, there is no time to waste, according to analysts.

They said that upgrading the country's ill-trained labour pool -- a historic barrier to development and foreign investment -- must become a top priority for Cambodia ahead of joining ASEAN along with sister observer nations Laos and Burma.

An Indonesian official said a visit to Phnom Penh starting on Monday by Indonesia's President Suharto was not related to ASEAN membership, although Asian diplomatic sources said there was "some symbolism" in the trip.

The regional grouping, which includes Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, plans to admit Cambodia, Laos and Burma simultaneously, as early as July of this year.
"We're in a constant state of learning and re-learning," said Kao Kim Hourn, director of the think tank, the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace.
"Ultimately, human resources development is a long-term process that we must start now... We see young faces learning about ASEAN, and they will be the dynamic of Cambodia's integration," he said.

After decades of civil war, Cambodia's educational system is notoriously overburdened and corrupt. The average child does less than four years in school, and only one third of children over the age of seven attend any educational institution.
Those problems are compounded by language barriers. Many students who studied at university learned French, and most who studied abroad went to the former Soviet Union or Eastern Europe.

"In primary school in the 1960s, we learned French, and now we must learn English. Overseas, others learned Russian, German, Dutch, Bulgarian," said Uy Sambath, acting director of the Ministry of Finance ASEAN department.
Three young men in his department said they spent seven years studying in Moscow and have since had to rush to learn English.
You Ay, director general of the general department of ASEAN at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said she has made improved education her priority.

In the past two years, she has sent about 250 Cambodians abroad for English and ASEAN training and another 250 have attended classes in-country, all funded by the United Nations, ASEAN, the European Union, Japan, Canada and New Zealand.
It is an effort in scholarship that Cambodia can ill afford to fail, You Ay said.
"We have an obligation to train our people to be capable -- in discussion, in negotiation, in protecting Cambodia's interests," she said.
"It's hard work for us, but we hope we can do it step by step."
